name: Wei Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ride a 125 scooter around the city centre, mostly food orders from lunch till late, and small parcels on quiet afternoons. I log on at half eleven near the noodle places on Canal Street because that's where the first orders come. I'm still slow at finding the back doors of restaurants, five months in, and the regulars at the burger place laugh at me. I like the movement and the bits of chat at the counter, and I don't like the rain or the drunk customers after eleven.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the money work out for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Better than you'd think, because I do the late shifts with the surge pay, so I'm on the higher end for riders. I lived cheap for years and have about eight months saved, plus a small index fund my uncle started for me when I was a kid. My boyfriend Sam is a primary school teacher, so we've got two incomes and a cheap flat. I'm not rich, but I'm not scared of a bad week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably make a joke in the riders' group chat, something like 'the robots aren't coming, but the rain still is.' I'd say it's a relief for workers and a bit embarrassing for the tech bosses who promised the moon. I'd still say the apps need regulating, robots or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means more of the same, and more of the same is fine. I'm learning the city, my times are getting better, the money's decent. I'd keep looking at an electrician course over the next couple of years, but there'd be no rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the late shifts and keep saving a few hundred a month. I'd probably finally ask my mate Kofi, who did an electrician course last year, how hard it really was. If two or three of us went for it together, I'd sign up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Like checking the forecast and seeing it's just a normal week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job that worries you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The usual stuff. My knee clicks on cold nights. One bad crash on the scooter could take me off the road for months, AI or no AI. And the app could cut the surge rate whenever it wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I used a chatbot to help me write a complaint to the app when they docked me for a late order that wasn't my fault. It wrote a better letter than I would have, and I got the money back. That's about the limit of it.

say: I'd joke that the **robots aren't coming**, but the rain still is.
I'd still say the **apps need regulating**, with or without AI.
think: More of the same is **fine for me**, because I'm still learning the city.
An **electrician course** stays on my list, with no rush.
do: Keep doing the **late shifts** for surge pay and save a few hundred monthly.
Ask **Kofi** how hard his electrician course really was.
Sign up only if **two or three friends** go together.
feel: **Calm**, like checking the forecast and finding a normal week.
S0.quote: One bad crash on the scooter could take me off the road for months, AI or no AI.
fieldNote: His **strong savings**, a fund and Sam's salary make this picture feel secure.
Ordinary risks like **crashes and surge cuts** are his real worries.
Typically **steady**: he'd only retrain once friends have proved it works.
Uses a **chatbot** occasionally for practical jobs like complaint letters.

steps.text: Keep the late food shifts around Canal Street for the surge pay
Put a few hundred a month into savings and the index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the usual story: the bosses get the savings and the workers get the stress. I'd share stuff online about making the apps pay a fair minimum per hour. With friends I'd say riders are lucky, because nobody's built a robot that can get up the steep hill by the canal on ice with a bag of noodles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm alright for a few years, because my job is mostly arms and legs. But Sam's job has a lot of planning and marking, and I'd wonder what happens to that. And I'd think the electrician course just got more urgent, because I don't want to be a rider at forty anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Kofi properly and probably start the evening electrical course in the autumn, keeping the late shifts going on weekends. I'd use AI a bit more, maybe to help with the theory homework. I'd keep the savings untouched as the safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for this year, but for the direction of things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier the apps need regulating. Does this picture change what you'd push for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, more than before. I'd push for a minimum hourly rate and a human you can appeal to. If software's doing the planning and the customer service, someone has to answer for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your day would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bit I don't do, really, the dispatch and the customer chat. The app already tells me where to go. The part with the scooter and the stairs and the cold soup is all mine for now.

say: I'd say the **bosses get the savings** while workers get the stress.
I'd share posts pushing for a **fair hourly minimum** for app riders.
think: My job is mostly **arms and legs**, so I'm fine for a few years.
The **electrician course** becomes more urgent, because I don't want to ride at forty.
do: Start the **evening electrical course** in the autumn while riding weekends.
Use **AI a bit more** to help with the course theory homework.
Keep the **savings untouched** as a safety net.
feel: **Uneasy** about the direction of things, though not about this year.
S1.quote: Nobody's built a robot that can get up the steep hill by the canal on ice with a bag of noodles.
fieldNote: He sees his day as **hands-on** and the app's side as the thinking part.
Worries about Sam's **teaching work** as much as his own.
The scenario **speeds up** a retraining plan he already had.
Progressive instincts show in wanting a **human appeal** and a minimum rate.

steps.text: Enrol in the evening electrical installation course this autumn
Use a chatbot to help with the course theory homework
Share campaigns for a minimum hourly rate for app riders
Leave the eight months of savings untouched as a safety net

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment governments have to act, with real money for people who lose work. Online I'd be the one sharing every article about a basic income. At work I'd say, half joking, enjoy the soup runs while they last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the riding is gone by 2031, maybe 2030 in the centre. I'm twenty-seven, so I'd be thirty-one with no trade unless I move now. I'm not broke, which helps, but it would sit on my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the electrician course straight away instead of waiting for the autumn, and cut riding to three nights a week. I'd move some of the index fund into plain savings so it can't crash. I'd join the riders' union too, because if we're going to bargain for anything, it has to be now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Not panic, but like the floor got steeper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If robots come around 2031, does being an electrician actually protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope so, for a while. Someone has to fit and fix all the chargers and machines for these robots, at least at first. But if robots can do hands-on work as well as people by 2031, I don't know how long that lasts either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sam talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly, and whether his school job is safe. We'd sit with the laptop and work out how long we could manage on one income. I'd probably say we should hold off on the deposit for a flat for a couple of years.

say: I'd say governments must act now with **real money** for displaced workers.
Online I'd share every article about a **basic income**.
think: I think the **riding is gone** by 2031, maybe sooner in the city centre.
I'm not broke, but having **no trade** at thirty-one would weigh on me.
do: Start the **electrician course** right away and cut riding to three nights.
Move part of the **index fund** into plain savings.
Join the **riders' union** so drivers bargain together while they can.
feel: **Tight in the chest**, not panic, as if the floor got steeper.
S2.quote: Someone has to fit and fix all the chargers and machines for these robots, at least at first.
fieldNote: He expects the **job to go** within five years but has a concrete plan.
Sees electrician work as a **bridge**, not a permanent safe place.
Household thinking turns to **Sam's school** job and the flat deposit.
Moves from steady to **acting quickly** when the timeline is short.

steps.text: Start the electrician course straight away and ride three nights
Join the riders' union branch in the city centre
Put the flat deposit plan on hold for two years
Move part of the index fund into a plain savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them, and push for training money now. I'd tell the group chat to stop pretending and start looking at courses. I'd still be cross with the companies, but less frantic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I've got time to do the electrician thing properly. By 2034 I could be qualified and a few years in. That's a different feeling from scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the course in the autumn like I planned, part-time over two years, riding four nights. Then I'd look for an apprentice spot with a local firm and drop riding. I'd keep the index fund where it is and keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit anxious underneath. More like a deadline than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change compared with the last one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to finish a course and get some real hours before the robots turn up. With two years I'd be rushing and maybe picking the wrong thing. With five I can watch what Kofi does first and copy what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who among the riders would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older ones, like Marek, who's been riding for fifteen years and doesn't read English well. He's got kids and no savings. I'd want the union to have something for people like him.

I'd tell the riders' group to **stop pretending** and look at courses.
think: Five years gives me time to do the **electrician course** properly.
Being **qualified by 2034** feels very different from scrambling.
do: Do the **part-time course** over two years while riding four nights.
Look for an **apprentice spot** with a local firm, then stop riding.
Keep the **index fund** invested and keep saving.
feel: **Uneasy** with some anxiety underneath, like a deadline rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to finish a course and get some real hours before the robots turn up.
fieldNote: The extra years turn **scramble into plan** for him.
He'd copy what works for **Kofi** first, true to his steady nature.
Shows care for older riders like **Marek** with no savings.
Still expects to **leave riding**, so the worry stays real.

steps.text: Take the part-time electrical course over two years
Apply for an electrician apprentice spot with a local firm
Keep saving each month and leave the index fund invested

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if governments use it well, and I'd vote for whoever has a plan. I'd still post about rights for gig workers. I'd tell friends it's not doom, it's homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I'd be thirty-seven when the robots arrive, hopefully a qualified electrician by then. I'd think about Sam and his school more than myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding for a year or two and save hard. Then I'd do the course at a normal pace, once Kofi's finished and told me how it went. I'd check now and then what AI tools sparkies are using and learn them when everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit uneasy, the way you feel about getting old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Where do you see yourself in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wiring houses, maybe with my own van. With Sam, maybe a kid, maybe a dog. I'd hope by then delivery riding is a story I tell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd leave it too late with that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's the risk for me. With ten years to prepare I'd keep saying next year, so I'd need my boyfriend or my mate Kofi to kick me.

I'd **vote** for whoever has a plan for gig workers.
think: I'd hopefully be a **qualified electrician** by the time robots arrive.
I'd think more about **Sam's school job** than my own.
do: Keep **riding** a year or two and **save hard**.
Do the **electrician course** at a normal pace after Kofi finishes.
Learn **AI tools** electricians use once others have tried them.

fieldNote: A decade feels **comfortable** given his savings, age and plan.

Relies on **Sam and Kofi** to keep him moving.

steps.text: Ride for one or two more years and save hard
Start the electrician course after Kofi finishes his
Vote for parties with a plan for gig workers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to finish anything before the robots came for the riding. What would help is free training while you still earn, so I could do the electrician course without losing three nights' pay. And a minimum rate on the apps so the last years aren't a race to the bottom.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the partners. Everyone talks about the worker, but we decide things together. Nobody makes a choice like retraining alone, because my boyfriend's job changes too.

headlineQuote: Nobody makes a choice like retraining alone, because my boyfriend's job changes too.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old** scooter rider who delivers food and parcels in the city centre.
He has **eight months saved**, a small index fund and a teacher boyfriend, Sam.
He's **steady**: he'd follow his friend Kofi into an electrician course once it's proven.
He blames **app bosses** and wants regulation and a basic income.
He stays calm in slow pictures but becomes **anxious** when robots arrive within five years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the riding would end before he could finish a trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Free training** that lets him study without losing paid shifts.
A **minimum rate** on the apps so the final years aren't a race to the bottom.
